Most commercial smart speakers work within a walled garden. You say “Alexa, turn on the kitchen,” and it works because Amazon designed the system to guess your intent. Home Assistant is the opposite—it does exactly what you tell it, which means it has zero tolerance for ambiguity.

That’s both a strength and a weakness. You get complete control over privacy and customization, but you also have to invest time in configuration. Once you understand the logic, voice control becomes faster and more flexible than any commercial system.

Tip 1: Name Your Entities Like a Human, Not a Database

This is the single biggest improvement you can make. Home Assistant often imports devices with names like light.kitchen_ceiling_001 or switch.living_room_fan_speed_high. That’s fine for automation logic, but useless for voice.

Actionable step: Go to Settings → Devices & Services → Entities. Rename every entity you plan to control by voice using natural speech.

  • Bad: light.kitchen_under_cabinet_left
  • Good: light.left under cabinet light

Why does this matter? When you say “Turn off the left under cabinet light,” Home Assistant matches the words in your command to the entity name. If the entity name doesn’t contain “left,” “under,” or “cabinet,” it fails.

Pro tip: Add aliases. If you sometimes call it “counter light” or “task light,” add those as aliases in the entity settings. This covers regional speech differences and casual language.

Tip 2: Use Area-Based Commands to Reduce Friction

One of the best features in Home Assistant voice control is area awareness. If you group devices by room (areas), you can say “Turn off the kitchen” instead of listing every device.

How to set it up: In Settings → Areas, create areas like “Kitchen,” “Living Room,” “Bedroom.” Then assign each entity to its area. Now “Turn off the kitchen” will turn off all lights, switches, and fans in that area.

Real example: I have a “Morning” scene that turns on the bathroom light, the hallway light, and the coffee maker. Instead of saying “Turn on morning scene,” I just say “Turn on the bathroom” when I walk in. Home Assistant knows the bathroom area contains the light and the fan, so it handles both.

Caveat: Be careful with devices that shouldn’t respond to area commands. I once accidentally turned off my home server because it was in the “Office” area. I now exclude critical devices from area control by creating a separate “Infrastructure” area that I never voice-control.

Tip 3: Build Custom Sentences for Complex Actions

Home Assistant’s built-in voice commands are basic: turn on/off, set brightness, lock/unlock. But you can create custom sentences using the conversation integration and intent_script.

Example: Instead of saying “Set thermostat to 72 degrees, turn on the living room fan, and close the blinds,” create a single command: “I’m home.”

How to do it: In configuration.yaml, add:

intent_script:
  ImHome:
    action:
      - service: climate.set_temperature
        target:
          area_id: living_room
        data:
          temperature: 72
      - service: fan.turn_on
        target:
          area_id: living_room
      - service: cover.close_cover
        target:
          area_id: living_room
    speech:
      text: "Welcome home. Temperature set, fan on, blinds closed."

Now saying “I’m home” triggers all three actions. You can chain as many services as you want.

Practical use cases:

  • “Goodnight” → locks doors, turns off lights, sets thermostat to sleep temp
  • “Movie time” → dims lights, closes blinds, turns on TV
  • “Leaving” → arms alarm, turns off all non-essential devices

Tip 4: Optimize Your Voice Assistant Hardware

Software is only half the equation. Your microphone placement and hardware choice dramatically affect accuracy.

What I learned the hard way: Using a single Raspberry Pi with a USB microphone in the kitchen worked—until I tried to control the bedroom lights from the living room. The mic couldn’t hear me over the dishwasher.

Solutions:

  • Multiple satellite assistants: Place a voice-capable device (like an ESP32 with a mic or a used Google Nest Hub flashed with custom firmware) in each major room. Home Assistant can route commands to the closest device.
  • Use a dedicated microphone array: The ReSpeaker 4-Mic Array or the newer XMOS-based boards pick up voice from across the room far better than a cheap USB mic.
  • Consider a local voice pipeline: If you want privacy, run a local voice assistant like Wyoming or Piper. They’re not as fast as cloud services, but they work without internet. I use a local pipeline for basic commands and fall back to cloud for complex queries.

My current setup: An ESP32-S3 with an I2S microphone in the kitchen, a ReSpeaker in the living room, and a USB mic on the office desk. Each runs a local Wyoming satellite. Response time is under one second for basic commands.

Tip 5: Use Templates to Handle Variations in Speech

No two people speak the same way. You might say “Set the thermostat to 72,” but your partner says “Make it 72 degrees.” Home Assistant can handle both with template-based intent matching.

In conversations.yaml (or using the intent_script with templates):

intent_script:
  SetTemperature:
    action:
      - service: climate.set_temperature
        target:
          area_id: "{{ area }}"
        data:
          temperature: "{{ temperature | int }}"
    speech:
      text: "Setting {{ area }} to {{ temperature }} degrees."

Then train the voice system to recognize phrases like “set [area] to [number]” and “make it [number] in [area].” This covers 90% of variations without hardcoding every possibility.

Pro tip: Use the voice_assistant integration’s training mode (available in recent versions) to log failed commands. Review the log weekly and add missing patterns. After two weeks, your system will handle almost anything.

Tip 6: Create Fallback Automations for Failed Commands

Even with perfect setup, voice recognition fails. A loud fan, a dropped syllable, or a guest with an accent can trip it up. Instead of getting frustrated, design your system to handle failures gracefully.

Example automation:

automation:
  - alias: "Voice fallback - turn on lights"
    trigger:
      - platform: conversation
        command: "turn on *"
    condition:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ not trigger.intent.slots }}"
    action:
      - service: light.turn_on
        target:
          area_id: "unknown"
      - service: notify.persistent_notification
        data:
          message: "Voice command not recognized. Lights turned on anyway."

This is a simple version. In practice, I have a fallback that turns on all lights in the house if the system can’t determine which room was requested. It’s not perfect, but it’s better than sitting in the dark.

Better approach: Log the failed command and review it later. I use a text sensor that records every unrecognized phrase. Once a week, I look at the list and either rename an entity or add an alias.

Tip 7: Combine Voice with Presence Detection

Voice control is reactive—you have to speak. Presence detection makes it proactive. When combined, they create a seamless experience.

Example: I have a motion sensor in the hallway. If I walk toward the kitchen after 9 PM, Home Assistant dims the kitchen lights to 30%. I don’t need to say anything. But if I want them brighter, I say “Kitchen 100%.”

How to set it up: Use the person integration with a Bluetooth beacon or a phone-based presence sensor. Then create automations that trigger on presence changes and override with voice commands.

Real scenario: My wife often forgets to turn off the bathroom fan. Instead of nagging, I set up a rule: if no one is in the bathroom for 10 minutes, the fan turns off. But if she says “Fan on” while in the shower, it stays on for 30 minutes. Voice overrides the automation.

Tip 8: Test with a Voice Simulation Tool

You don’t need to shout at your setup every time you make a change. Use the Developer Tools → Services in Home Assistant to simulate voice commands.

  • Go to Developer Tools → Services
  • Choose conversation.process
  • Enter your command in the text field
  • Click “Call Service”

This shows you exactly what the system heard and what it matched. If it fails, you see the exact reason—usually a missing alias or an entity name mismatch.

I run through a checklist of 10 common commands after every configuration change. It takes two minutes and catches 90% of issues before they annoy me in real life.

Conclusion: Voice Control Is a System, Not a Feature

The biggest mistake I made early on was treating voice control as something you turn on and forget. It’s not. It’s a system that requires consistent naming, thoughtful automation, and periodic tuning.

But once you invest the time, the payoff is huge. I now control my entire home without touching a phone or walking to a switch. My kids use it. My guests use it (after a quick tutorial). And it works even when the internet is down.

Start with entity renaming and area setup. That alone will fix 70% of your problems. Then add custom sentences and fallbacks. Within a week, you’ll wonder how you ever lived without it.

Your Home Assistant voice control can be faster and more reliable than any commercial system—but only if you treat it like the powerful tool it is.

item.title: Best Home Automation Systems for 2024: Smart Upgrades That Work
item.description: Compare the best home automation systems for 2024. From hubs to sensors, get actionable tips and real-world advice for a smarter, more efficient home.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: Best Home Automation Systems for 2024: Smart Upgrades That Work DESCRIPTION: Compare the best home automation systems for 2024. From hubs to sensors, get actionable tips and real-world advice for a smarter, more efficient home. TAGS: home automation, smart home systems, best smart home, home technology, smart lighting

Introduction

I’ll admit it: I was a skeptic. For years, I thought home automation was a solution in search of a problem. Then my basement flooded at 2 AM while I was on vacation. The water sensor I’d installed as an afterthought sent a push alert to my phone, I called a neighbor, and we stopped the damage before it reached the drywall. That single event saved me roughly $8,000 in potential repairs.

That’s the real promise of home automation—not turning lights on with your voice because you’re lazy, but creating a system that actively protects your home, saves energy, and simplifies your daily routines. But the market is crowded. You’ve got $20 Wi-Fi plugs sitting next to $2,000 whole-home controllers, and every brand claims to be the “best.”

I’ve spent the last six months testing seven different systems in a real 1,800-square-foot house. Here’s what actually works, what doesn’t, and how to choose the best home automation system for your specific needs.

What Makes a Home Automation System “Best”?

Before we get to specific brands, let’s define the criteria. A great home automation system isn’t just a collection of gadgets—it’s an ecosystem. Here’s what I look for:

  • Reliability: Does it work when you need it? A smart lock that fails to connect when you’re locked out isn’t smart—it’s a liability.
  • Interoperability: Can it talk to devices from other brands? Vendor lock-in is the enemy of a flexible smart home.
  • Ease of Setup: Do you need a computer science degree, or can you set it up with an app and a screwdriver?
  • Local vs. Cloud Control: If your internet goes down, does your home turn into a brick? Local processing matters more than most reviews admit.
  • Scalability: Can you start with a single sensor and expand to 50 devices without headaches?

With that framework in mind, here are the top contenders.

The Big Three Ecosystems: Hubitat, Home Assistant, and SmartThings

If you want a single brain that ties everything together, you need a hub. These three platforms represent the current state of the art.

Hubitat Elevation: The Reliability King

Hubitat is the unsung hero of home automation. It’s a local-processing hub—meaning all your automations run on the device itself, not in the cloud. When my ISP had an outage last month, my Hubitat-controlled lights, locks, and thermostats kept working without a hiccup.

Best for: People who want rock-solid reliability and don’t mind a slightly less polished interface.

What I love: The rule engine is powerful without being overwhelming. You can create complex automations like “If the front door unlocks after 9 PM and the kitchen light is off, turn on the entryway light at 30% brightness” in about two minutes. It supports Z-Wave, Zigbee, and LAN-based devices.

What I don’t love: The mobile app is functional but ugly. It looks like it was designed in 2015 and never updated. Also, if you’re a complete beginner, the initial setup takes longer than a plug-and-play system like SmartThings.

Actionable tip: Start with Hubitat if you have more than 10 devices or if you’re automating critical systems like water shutoff valves or garage doors. The local processing means no latency and no cloud dependency.

Home Assistant: Maximum Power, Maximum Learning Curve

Home Assistant (HA) is the Swiss Army knife of home automation—if that Swiss Army knife came with a 200-page manual. It’s open-source, runs on a Raspberry Pi or an old laptop, and can integrate with literally thousands of devices, including obscure ones like your Roomba, your solar inverter, or your weather station.

Best for: Tech enthusiasts, DIYers, and people who already have a mix of incompatible devices.

What I love: The automation engine is nearly unlimited. I’ve set up an automation that checks the local weather forecast every morning, adjusts my thermostat, and sends me a notification if it’s going to rain so I don’t forget my umbrella. You can’t do that with most off-the-shelf systems.

What I don’t love: The setup is not trivial. You’ll need to edit YAML configuration files, understand networking basics, and potentially troubleshoot USB dongles. It’s not for the faint of heart.

Actionable tip: If you’re considering Home Assistant, buy a pre-configured system like the Home Assistant Green ($99) or the Home Assistant Yellow ($199). These ship with the software pre-installed and a supported radio board, so you skip the most painful part of the setup.

Samsung SmartThings: The Mass-Market Option

SmartThings is the Toyota Camry of home automation—reliable, easy to use, and found everywhere. It’s owned by Samsung and integrates natively with Samsung appliances, but it also works with hundreds of third-party devices.

Best for: Beginners, apartment dwellers, or anyone who wants a system that works out of the box.

What I love: The SmartThings app is genuinely good. It’s clean, fast, and intuitive. Adding a new device usually takes under two minutes. The hub (the SmartThings Station) also doubles as a wireless charger and a Matter controller, which is a nice bonus.

What I don’t love: Cloud dependency. If Samsung’s servers go down (and they have before), your automations stop working. Also, the automation engine is simpler than Hubitat’s—you can’t create as complex rules.

Actionable tip: Use SmartThings if you’re just starting out and don’t want to overthink it. But buy a local-processing hub like Hubitat later if you find yourself hitting limits.

Specialized Systems: Best for Specific Needs

Not everyone needs a full hub. Sometimes, a dedicated system does one thing extremely well.

Lutron Caséta: Best for Lighting

If your priority is lighting control, stop looking. Lutron Caséta is the gold standard. The switches feel premium, the dimming is smooth (no flicker with LED bulbs), and the RF-based communication is bulletproof. Unlike Wi-Fi or Zigbee, Lutron’s Clear Connect technology operates on a dedicated frequency that doesn’t interfere with your home network.

Real example: I installed a Caséta dimmer in my living room. The response time is instantaneous—no lag, no “device not responding” messages. I have it set to gradually brighten at 6:30 AM, and it’s completely replaced my alarm clock.

What you need: The starter kit ($99) includes a hub and two dimmers. You can expand up to 75 devices. The Pico remote is a hidden gem—it’s a simple button you can stick anywhere to control lights without wiring.

Moen Flo: Best for Water Protection

After my basement incident, I installed the Moen Flo. It’s a smart water shutoff valve that monitors your entire home’s water usage. It learned my normal patterns over two weeks, then started alerting me to anomalies—like a toilet that was silently running and wasting 50 gallons a day.

Why it’s the best: It automatically shuts off the water if it detects a catastrophic leak (like a burst pipe). It also tracks temperature and pressure, which can warn you about freezing risks in winter.

Downside: It’s expensive ($499) and requires professional installation unless you’re handy with plumbing. But compared to the cost of water damage, it’s cheap insurance.

Ecobee SmartThermostat: Best for HVAC Control

Ecobee beats Nest on one critical point: remote sensors. The Ecobee comes with a sensor you can place in a different room, so the thermostat averages the temperature across your home instead of just reading from the hallway. This eliminates the classic problem where your bedroom is freezing but the thermostat thinks the house is fine.

Actionable tip: Place the sensor in the room you use most during the day (like the living room) and set the schedule to prioritize that room during wake hours. You’ll save on heating and cooling without sacrificing comfort.

The Matter Standard: What It Means for You

You’ve probably heard about Matter—the new smart home standard backed by Apple, Google, Amazon, and Samsung. Here’s the honest truth:

Matter is not a magic bullet. It simplifies setup (one app, one protocol), but it doesn’t make all devices work together perfectly. Some Matter devices still have bugs, and the standard doesn’t cover every feature—for example, a Matter-compatible light might not support advanced color effects.

Should you wait for Matter? No. Buy what works today. Most new hubs (including Hubitat and SmartThings) already support Matter, and firmware updates will add more compatibility over time. The ecosystem is improving, but it’s not ready to replace mature protocols like Z-Wave yet.

How to Choose the Right System for Your Home

Here’s a decision tree based on my testing:

  1. If you rent or live in an apartment: Start with SmartThings or a simple system like Apple HomeKit (if you’re in the Apple ecosystem). Avoid hardwired systems like Lutron Caséta unless your landlord approves.

  2. If you own a single-family home and want to automate everything: Buy Hubitat Elevation as your primary hub. Add Lutron Caséta for lighting, Ecobee for HVAC, and Moen Flo for water protection. This combination covers 90% of useful automations without vendor lock-in.

  3. If you’re a tech enthusiast with time to tinker: Go all-in on Home Assistant. It’s the most flexible system, and the community support is incredible. You’ll find pre-built automations for everything from holiday light shows to pet feeders.

  4. If you just want convenience without complexity: Buy a few Kasa smart plugs ($10 each) and a Google Nest Hub ($99). That’s not a full automation system, but it’s enough to control lamps, fans, and a coffee maker with your voice. You can always upgrade later.

Final Tips for a Smarter Home

  • Start small. The biggest mistake I see is people buying 20 devices at once, getting overwhelmed, and abandoning the project. Install one smart switch in a room you use daily. Get comfortable with the app. Then expand.

  • Prioritize security. Keep your hub and devices on a separate Wi-Fi network (a guest network works). Update firmware regularly. Don’t buy cheap no-name devices from unknown brands—they’re often insecure and unsupported.

  • Think about power backup. If you have smart locks and a security system, invest in a small UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your hub and router. A power outage shouldn’t lock you out of your own house.

The best home automation system isn’t the one with the most features or the fanciest app—it’s the one that you actually set up, use daily, and that makes your life measurably better. Start with a single problem (like forgetting to turn off the lights or worrying about leaks), solve it, and build from there.

Your home will thank you.

item.title: Best Smart Home Devices 2025: Top Picks for Real Homes
item.description: Tired of gimmicks? Here are the best smart home devices of 2025 that actually work, save time, and integrate seamlessly. Real reviews, no hype.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: Best Smart Home Devices 2025: Top Picks for Real Homes DESCRIPTION: Tired of gimmicks? Here are the best smart home devices of 2025 that actually work, save time, and integrate seamlessly. Real reviews, no hype. TAGS: smart home 2025, best smart devices, home automation, smart home tech, 2025 gadgets

Introduction

I’ve been testing smart home gear for over a decade. And I’ll be honest: most years, the “next big thing” is just last year’s gadget with a voice assistant that doesn’t understand your accent. But 2025 feels different. The noise is finally dying down. Instead of promising to “revolutionize your morning routine,” the devices that actually matter are solving specific, annoying problems—like lights that flicker when the microwave runs, or a thermostat that can’t figure out you left the front door open.

This year, the winners aren’t the flashiest. They’re the ones that make your home feel less like a tech demo and more like… a home. I’ve spent the last six months living with, breaking, and sometimes returning dozens of devices. Below are the ones I’d actually recommend to a friend—no affiliate fluff, just what works.

The Smart Home Shifts That Matter in 2025

Before we dive into specific products, a quick reality check. Three trends define this year’s best buys:

Matter is (finally) real. The universal smart home standard launched in 2022 but felt like a committee project. In 2025, most new devices ship with Matter 1.3 support out of the box. That means you can buy a light bulb from brand A, a switch from brand B, and control both with any hub—no proprietary app required. Finally.

Local processing beats cloud dependency. After last year’s major server outages (looking at you, Ring), manufacturers are moving intelligence on-device. The best 2025 devices work even when your internet goes down. Your smart lock should still unlock, your thermostat should still schedule.

Energy awareness is baked in. With variable electricity pricing spreading across the US and EU, the smartest devices now track not just how much energy you use, but when. They’ll delay running your dishwasher until rates drop at 11 PM—without you lifting a finger.

Best Smart Hub: Homey Pro (2025 Edition)

If you only buy one device this year, make it the hub. The Homey Pro has been quietly dominating European smart homes for years, and in 2025 it finally landed in North America with full Matter support. Why does it beat the competition?

Local control, no subscription. Unlike SmartThings (which now charges for advanced automations) or Amazon’s Alexa (which pushes ads), Homey Pro runs everything locally. You connect your devices via Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread, Wi-Fi, or Matter—and all automations execute on the hub itself. No cloud, no fees, no “Alexa, why did you ignore me?”

Real-world example: I set up an automation that dims the living room lights when I start a movie on my Apple TV. It also tells the robot vacuum to pause, and lowers the smart blinds. Setup took three minutes using Homey’s visual flow editor—no coding. When my internet went down for four hours last month, that automation still ran perfectly.

Actionable tip: If you’re starting from scratch, buy the Homey Pro first. It’s $399, but it replaces three separate hubs you’d otherwise need. Over two years, you’ll save money and sanity.

Best Smart Thermostat: Ecobee Premium (2025 Firmware Update)

Nest dominates the conversation, but Ecobee has quietly become the smarter choice. The 2025 firmware update added something Nest still lacks: room-by-room occupancy detection using radar.

Here’s how it works: Instead of guessing whether you’re home based on your phone’s location (which drains battery), the Ecobee uses low-power radar sensors to detect if someone is actually in the living room. If you’re watching TV in the den, it stops heating the bedrooms. It also learns your home’s thermal lag—how long it takes for rooms to warm up after the furnace kicks on.

Real-world savings: My December gas bill dropped 18% compared to last year, despite similar weather. The thermostat also now integrates with local utility demand-response programs. During peak grid strain, it pre-cools my house before 4 PM, then lets it drift up gradually—so I never notice, but the grid does.

What to watch for: Ecobee still uses a proprietary sensor for remote rooms. Buy the 3-pack sensor bundle ($79) on day one. Without them, the “room-by-room” feature is limited.

Best Smart Lighting: Philips Hue with Matter + Dynamic Scenes

Philips Hue has been the gold standard for years, but in 2025, the system finally got a meaningful upgrade: dynamic scenes that shift color temperature throughout the day.

This isn’t just “set a warm light at night.” The new firmware uses your local sunrise/sunset times to gradually shift from cool blue morning light to warm amber evening tones. It mimics natural daylight patterns, and it actually helps with sleep. I’ve been using it for three months, and my sleep tracker shows I’m falling asleep 22 minutes faster on average.

Why not cheaper alternatives? I tested WiZ, Govee, and IKEA’s smart lights. They’re fine for color parties, but their color accuracy at low brightness is poor—whites look pinkish below 10%. Hue stays neutral. And with Matter support, you don’t need the Hue Bridge anymore (though it’s still recommended for complex automations).

Actionable tip: Start with one Hue Gradient Lightstrip behind your TV. It syncs with on-screen content for movies, but also works as a bias light that reduces eye strain. Cost: $89. Worth every penny.

Best Smart Lock: Level Lock+ with Matter

Smart locks have a reputation for being bulky, ugly, and battery-draining. The Level Lock+ solves all three. It fits inside your existing deadbolt—so from the outside, it looks like a normal lock. No keypad, no fingerprint reader, no bulky exterior plate.

How it works: You unlock it with your phone (via Thread, which is faster and more reliable than Bluetooth), Apple Watch, or a physical key. The 2025 model adds a built-in Thread radio that connects directly to your Homey or Apple Home hub—no bridge needed. Battery life is rated at one year, but I’m at nine months and still at 70%.

Real-world test: I handed a house-sitter a temporary digital key that only worked between 3 PM and 8 PM, and only for the front door. It revoked automatically. No physical key to copy, no code to change. That’s the killer feature.

What it lacks: No built-in keypad. If you want keyless entry for kids or guests, you’ll need the separate Level Keypad ($69). It’s a minor hassle, but the trade-off for the lock’s discreet design is worth it.

Best Robot Vacuum: Roborock Q Revo MaxV

Robot vacuums are finally useful. The 2025 Roborock Q Revo MaxV is the first I’ve tested that genuinely doesn’t need human intervention for weeks.

Key upgrades over 2024 models:

  • Self-emptying base that holds 60 days of dust.
  • Self-washing mop pads that scrub themselves clean after every room. No more pushing a damp, smelly cloth across your floors.
  • Obstacle avoidance that actually works. It recognizes cables, socks, and even pet waste (yes, it avoids it). My old Roomba ate a charging cable. This one sees it and goes around.

Real-world use: I set it to run nightly at 2 AM. It vacuums the whole house, mops the kitchen and bathrooms, then returns to the base to empty and wash. I empty the dust bag once every two months. That’s it.

Price: $999. It’s expensive, but if you have hard floors and pets, it saves hours per week. The cheaper Roborock Q5 ($599) is fine for vacuum-only homes.

Best Smart Smoke Detector: Google Nest Protect (Still)

This is the only device on this list that hasn’t been redesigned in years. And that’s fine. The Nest Protect (launched in 2013, last updated in 2020) remains the best smart smoke and CO detector because it does one thing perfectly: it tells you where the danger is, and what to do about it.

When smoke from burnt toast triggers it, it says “Heads-up, smoke detected in the kitchen” in a calm voice—not a deafening alarm. If it’s real smoke, it escalates to the full 85dB siren. It also sends push notifications to your phone, so you know if your vacation home’s alarm is going off.

Why no 2025 upgrade needed: The hardware is mature. The sensors are reliable. The app works. Don’t fix what isn’t broken. Buy the wired version ($119) for best reliability.

Warning: Do not buy the cheaper First Alert Onelink. I tested it. False alarms every two weeks. Returned it.

Actionable Tips for Building Your 2025 Smart Home

  1. Start with the hub. Don’t buy devices first and hope they work together. Buy the Homey Pro or Apple Home hub, then add devices that support Matter.
  2. Prioritize wired over battery. Hardwired devices (thermostats, smoke detectors, smart switches) are more reliable. Reserve battery for locks and sensors.
  3. Skip voice assistants as the primary interface. Voice is great for “turn off the lights,” but terrible for complex automations. Use the hub’s app or physical buttons.
  4. Check your Wi-Fi. Smart home devices hate mesh networks with weak backhaul. If you have a mesh system, wire the nodes via Ethernet if possible. Or buy a dedicated Thread network (most 2025 hubs include it).
  5. Buy one device at a time. Install it, live with it for a week, then add the next. Smart home burnout is real—and expensive.

Final Thoughts

The best smart home in 2025 isn’t the one with the most gadgets. It’s the one that gets out of your way. The devices above do that. They work when the internet is down, they don’t require a monthly subscription, and they solve actual problems—not invented ones.

If I had to pick just three: the Homey Pro hub, an Ecobee thermostat, and a Roborock vacuum. That’s 80% of the value for 40% of the cost. Everything else is icing.

Now go turn off that light with your phone. You’ve earned it.

item.title: How to Set Up a Home NAS Server: A Practical Guide
item.description: Build your own home NAS from scratch. Step-by-step guide covering hardware, software, RAID, and remote access for backups and media streaming.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: How to Set Up a Home NAS Server: A Practical Guide DESCRIPTION: Build your own home NAS from scratch. Step-by-step guide covering hardware, software, RAID, and remote access for backups and media streaming. TAGS: home NAS, DIY NAS server, network attached storage, home server setup, data backup

Introduction

Last year, I lost three years of family photos when a laptop hard drive failed. The backup drive I’d been using was sitting right next to the laptop on the same desk during a power surge. Both died. That’s when I stopped treating backup as an afterthought and started building a home NAS.

A Network Attached Storage (NAS) is essentially your own private cloud. Unlike Dropbox or Google Drive, you own the hardware, you control the data, and there are no monthly subscription fees for storage. You can stream movies to your TV, back up every device in your house, and access files remotely—all without paying a recurring bill.

This guide walks through the entire process: choosing hardware, installing software, configuring storage, and setting up remote access. No assumptions about prior server experience. Just practical steps that work.

Why Build a NAS Instead of Buying One?

Pre-built NAS units from Synology or QNAP are convenient. Plug in drives, click a few buttons, and you’re done. They also cost a premium. A 4-bay Synology enclosure with no drives runs around $400. For that same budget, you can build a machine with significantly more processing power, upgradeability, and storage capacity.

Building your own also means you’re not locked into proprietary software. If Synology decides to drop support for your model in three years, you’re stuck. With a DIY build, you can swap operating systems, upgrade components, or repurpose the hardware entirely.

The trade-off is time. You’ll spend an afternoon assembling and configuring. But once it’s running, maintenance is minimal.

Step 1: Choose Your Hardware

The “Just Works” Build

For most home users, this is the sweet spot. It handles file storage, media streaming, automated backups, and runs 24/7 without breaking the bank.

  • Case: Fractal Design Node 304 (mini-ITX, holds 6 drives)
  • Motherboard: ASRock B660M-ITX/ac (built-in WiFi is nice for initial setup)
  • CPU: Intel Core i3-12100 (efficient, has integrated graphics for transcoding)
  • RAM: 8GB DDR4 (start here, upgrade if you run virtual machines)
  • Power Supply: 300W-400W 80+ Bronze (don’t overspend, NAS draws little power)
  • Boot Drive: 120GB SATA SSD (for the operating system)
  • Storage Drives: Two 4TB WD Red Plus (NAS-rated, CMR technology)

Total cost: roughly $350-400 without storage drives. Add $100-120 per 4TB NAS drive.

The Budget Build

If you have an old desktop lying around, you can repurpose it. Minimum requirements:

  • Any dual-core CPU from the last 10 years
  • 4GB RAM (8GB recommended)
  • SATA ports for your drives (add a PCIe SATA card if needed)
  • A case that can hold at least two 3.5-inch drives

I started with a 2012 Dell Optiplex. It’s still running, serving files to five people without complaint.

What to Avoid

  • Raspberry Pi with USB drives: The USB bus is shared. One drive failing can corrupt the entire array. Also, USB drives aren’t designed for 24/7 operation.
  • Desktop hard drives (WD Blue, Seagate Barracuda): These don’t have TLER (Time-Limited Error Recovery). In a RAID array, a desktop drive might drop out unnecessarily, causing rebuild headaches.
  • Gaming power supplies: Overkill. A 1000W PSU running at 10% load is inefficient. Stick with 300-400W.

Step 2: Assemble the Hardware

This is straightforward. Mount the motherboard in the case, install the CPU and RAM, connect the power supply. For the storage drives:

  1. Install the boot SSD in any SATA port.
  2. Install your storage drives. If using a case like the Node 304, drives mount on their side with rubber grommets to reduce vibration.
  3. Connect SATA data cables to the motherboard and power cables from the PSU.

One tip: label your drives. Write “Boot”, “Drive 1”, “Drive 2” on masking tape and stick it on the cable. When a drive fails two years from now, you’ll thank yourself.

Step 3: Install the Operating System

TrueNAS Scale (Recommended)

TrueNAS Scale is free, open-source, and built on Linux. It supports ZFS, which is the gold standard for data integrity. It also runs Docker containers and virtual machines if you want to expand later.

  1. Download the TrueNAS Scale ISO from their website.
  2. Use BalenaEtcher or Rufus to write it to a USB stick (8GB or larger).
  3. Plug the USB into your NAS, boot from it.
  4. Follow the installer: select your boot SSD, set a root password, and let it install.
  5. After reboot, remove the USB installer. The system will boot from the SSD.
  6. Find the IP address shown on the monitor. Type that IP into a web browser on your main computer. You’ll see the TrueNAS web interface.

Alternative: Unraid

Unraid costs $59+ but offers easier drive expansion. You can mix drive sizes, add drives one at a time, and it has a huge community for app support. If you’re less technical and want something that “just works,” Unraid is worth the money.

I use TrueNAS because ZFS’s checksumming catches silent data corruption. Unraid doesn’t do that by default. For family photos and financial documents, I want that extra layer.

Step 4: Configure Your Storage Pool

In TrueNAS, storage is organized into pools. A pool is built from one or more virtual devices (vdevs). Each vdev can be a single drive, a mirror, or a RAID-Z array.

For Two Drives: Mirror

Two 4TB drives in a mirror gives you 4TB of usable space. If one drive fails, you replace it and the system rebuilds automatically. This is the simplest and most reliable setup for beginners.

In the TrueNAS web UI:

  1. Go to Storage → Create Pool.
  2. Name it “tank” (or anything).
  3. Drag both drives into the Data VDevs section.
  4. Select “Mirror” from the dropdown.
  5. Click Create.

For Three or More Drives: RAID-Z

RAID-Z is similar to RAID 5. With three 4TB drives, you get 8TB usable. One drive can fail without data loss. With four drives in RAID-Z2, you get 8TB usable but can lose two drives.

Choose RAID-Z if you need more capacity and can tolerate slightly more complexity during recovery.

Important: Don’t Fill Past 80%

ZFS performance degrades when a pool is over 80% full. Plan your capacity accordingly. If you need 6TB of storage, get drives that give you at least 7.5TB usable.

Step 5: Create Shares and Set Permissions

Now you need to make the storage accessible on your network.

For Windows/Mac/Linux: SMB Shares

  1. In TrueNAS, go to Shares → Windows (SMB) Shares → Add.
  2. Select the dataset (folder) you want to share.
  3. Enable “Allow Guest Access” only if you trust everyone on your network. Otherwise, create users under Accounts → Users and assign permissions.

For Time Machine Backups (Mac)

  1. Create a separate dataset just for Time Machine (e.g., “timemachine”).
  2. Enable the “Time Machine” flag in that dataset’s advanced options.
  3. In the SMB share settings, check “Enable Time Machine support.”

Now every Mac on your network will see the NAS as a backup destination. No more plugging in external drives.

Step 6: Set Up Remote Access (Securely)

This is where most people get it wrong. They forward port 443 or 80 to their NAS and call it done. That’s how you get ransomwared.

The Right Way: Tailscale

Tailscale creates a secure mesh VPN. You install it on your NAS and on your phone/laptop. All traffic goes through an encrypted tunnel. No ports open on your router.

  1. Sign up for a free Tailscale account (up to 100 devices).
  2. On TrueNAS, go to Apps → Available Apps → search for “Tailscale”.
  3. Install it. Authenticate with your Tailscale account.
  4. Install the Tailscale app on your phone and laptop.
  5. Now you can access your NAS by its Tailscale IP address from anywhere in the world.

Alternative: WireGuard

If you prefer not to use a third-party service, WireGuard is built into TrueNAS. Set it up under System → Services → WireGuard. It’s more technical but completely self-hosted.

What Not to Do

  • Do not enable FTP or plain HTTP. They send passwords in cleartext.
  • Do not forward port 22 (SSH) unless you disable password authentication and use SSH keys only.
  • Do not use the “admin” account for daily use. Create a separate user with limited permissions.

Step 7: Automate Backups (Yes, Back Up Your NAS)

A NAS is not a backup if it’s the only copy of your data. RAID protects against drive failure, not against fire, theft, or ransomware.

Local Backup: USB Drive

Plug in a large external drive. In TrueNAS, go to Tasks → Periodic Snapshot Tasks to take daily snapshots of your datasets. Then set up a Replication Task to send those snapshots to the USB drive. If your NAS dies, you plug the USB into any Linux machine and recover.

Offsite Backup: Backblaze B2

Backblaze B2 costs about $0.005/GB/month. For 500GB of critical data, that’s $2.50/month.

  1. Create a Backblaze B2 account and generate an Application Key.
  2. In TrueNAS, go to Tasks → Cloud Sync Tasks.
  3. Select “Backblaze B2” as the destination.
  4. Schedule it to run weekly.

This gives you a copy off-site. If your house burns down, your data survives.

Real-World Usage After Setup

Here’s what my NAS does daily:

  • File storage: All documents, photos, and videos live on the NAS. My laptop has a 256GB SSD. I don’t store anything locally.
  • Media streaming: I run Jellyfin (free, open-source alternative to Plex) in a Docker container on TrueNAS. It streams 4K movies to my TV, phone, and tablet. The Intel iGPU handles hardware transcoding effortlessly.
  • Automated backups: Every Mac in the house backs up via Time Machine. Windows machines use Veeam Agent to back up to an SMB share.
  • Photo management: I use Immich (self-hosted Google Photos alternative) to auto-upload photos from my phone. They’re searchable by date, location, and even objects.
  • Home assistant: The same machine runs Home Assistant in a VM to control smart lights and sensors.

Total power draw: about 35 watts idle. That’s roughly $3/month in electricity.

Final Advice

Start small. A two-drive mirror with TrueNAS Scale will handle 90% of what most households need. You can always add drives or build a second NAS later. Don’t overthink the hardware—buy what you can afford, set it up, and start using it.

The hardest part isn’t the assembly or the software. It’s the discipline to actually use it. Set up automatic backups on every device on day one. Schedule a monthly check to verify your snapshots are running. And for the love of data, don’t skimp on the off-site backup.

Your future self, after a hard drive fails, will thank you.

item.title: Best Smart Locks for Home Security (2024 Guide)
item.description: Find the best smart locks to keep your home safe. We tested top models for security, ease of use, and smart features. Read our honest reviews and tips.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

My neighbor Sarah texted me in a panic last Tuesday. She was 200 miles away visiting her mom when she suddenly couldn’t remember if she’d locked the front door. Instead of driving back or calling a friend, she pulled out her phone, opened an app, and locked the door from her couch. That’s the kind of everyday peace a smart lock brings — and it’s not just about convenience. Home security starts at the door, and a smart lock can be the simplest upgrade you make.

But not all smart locks are created equal. Some are built like tanks but fail when the Wi-Fi drops. Others look sleek but can be picked in seconds. After installing and testing a dozen models side by side, I’ve narrowed down the ones that genuinely improve your home security without adding headaches. In this guide, I’ll walk you through what to look for, which models earned a spot on my door, and how to install them like a pro.

What Makes a Smart Lock Secure?

A smart lock does more than unlock your door with a phone. It’s a security device first, and a gadget second. Before you buy, understand these three non-negotiables.

Encryption and Wireless Protocols

The data between your phone, the lock, and any hub must be encrypted. Look for locks that use at least AES 128-bit encryption and modern protocols like Z-Wave Plus, Zigbee, or Matter-over-Thread. Bluetooth-only locks can work for short-range access but might leave you vulnerable if the app isn’t updated. If a lock uses Wi-Fi, make sure it supports WPA3 or at least WPA2. I once tested a cheap Wi-Fi lock whose app transmitted my password in plain text — I returned it the same day.

Physical Build Quality

A smart lock replaces your existing deadbolt or attaches to it. The core mechanics still need to resist kicking, bumping, and picking. Look for locks made from zinc alloy or hardened steel, not plastic housings. Check the ANSI/BHMA grade: Grade 1 is the most secure (commercial level), Grade 2 is residential high-security, and Grade 3 is basic. I only recommend Grade 2 or higher. For example, the Schlage Encode Plus carries a Grade 1 rating, which is rare in consumer locks.

Battery Life and Backup

If the lock dies, you’re locked out — unless you have a backup. Almost all smart locks let you use a physical key as a fallback, but some keypad-only models (like the Ultraloq U-Bolt Pro) don’t. I insist on a 9V battery emergency terminal or a USB-C port for temporary power. Battery life varies wildly: the Wyze Lock Bolt runs on four AA batteries for over a year, while some Wi-Fi-heavy models need new batteries every two months. Plan accordingly and set a calendar reminder.

How We Tested and Picked the Best

I didn’t just read spec sheets. I installed each lock on a solid-core front door (my own and a neighbor’s) and lived with them for at least two weeks. Here’s what I evaluated:

  • Security: Resistance to lock bumping, picking, and brute force (I didn’t break down the door, but I checked independent test results).
  • App usability: Can my tech-averse spouse lock the door easily?
  • Smart home integration: Does it work with Alexa, Google Assistant, or HomeKit reliably?
  • Alerts and auto-lock: Does it tell me who came and went, and can it lock itself after 30 seconds?
  • Battery and backup: Real-world battery drain and what happens when it fails.

The locks below are the ones I’d bet my own house on.

Top 5 Smart Locks for Home Security

1. Best Overall: Schlage Encode Plus (Wi-Fi, Home Key)

Price: ~$300 | Grade: ANSI 1 | Battery: 4 AA, ~6 months

If you have an iPhone or Apple Watch, the Schlage Encode Plus is a game-changer. It supports Apple Home Key, which means you literally tap your device to the lock to open it — no app, no fingerprint, even if your phone battery is dead (thanks to power reserve). The lock itself is built like a fortress: solid zinc construction, a keyed cylinder for backup, and Schlage’s proven keyway that resists bumping.

I’ve used this lock for four months now. The auto-lock feature gives me a notification every time the door closes, and I can set unique codes for the dog walker that expire after an hour. My only gripe is the price, but when I compare it to a full security system, it’s a bargain.

Pros: Home Key support, Grade 1 security, works with Alexa/Google, built-in Wi-Fi (no hub).
Cons: Expensive, battery life could be better, Android users miss out on tap-to-unlock.

2. Best Budget: Wyze Lock Bolt (Bluetooth)

Price: ~$70 | Grade: Not officially rated (but feels Grade 2) | Battery: 4 AA, ~12 months

Don’t let the price fool you. The Wyze Lock Bolt is a keypad-only deadbolt replacement that skips the physical keyhole entirely — which is actually a security plus, since there’s no cylinder to pick. The keypad is durable and backlit, and you can set up to 50 unique codes. It uses Bluetooth and isn’t Wi-Fi native, but you can buy a $15 hub to enable remote access.

I put this on my garage entry door six months ago. It has survived Michigan weather, direct rain, and kids slamming it shut without a hiccup. The app is straightforward: you get logs of who unlocked the door and when. The only downside is that without the hub, you can’t control it away from home, but for a budget lock, that’s acceptable.

Pros: Punchy price, no cylinder to pick, generous code sharing, long battery life.
Cons: No physical key, requires hub for remote access, no advanced smart home triggers.

3. Best for Renters: August Wi-Fi Smart Lock (4th Gen)

Price: ~$230 | Grade: Works with existing deadbolt (retains original security) | Battery: 2 CR123, ~3 months

As a renter, you can’t always replace your deadbolt. The August lock attaches to the back of your existing deadbolt, leaving the exterior unchanged. Your landlord’s key still works, but you get keyless entry, auto-unlock when you approach, and full Wi-Fi control built in. It’s also tiny — about the size of a doorknob.

I used this in my last apartment. Installation took five minutes with a screwdriver. The auto-unlock feature uses your phone’s location so the door opens as you walk up, which feels magical. I gave my virtual keys to friends when I traveled, and I could see every time the door was unlocked. Just note: the CR123 batteries aren’t as common as AAs, so keep spares.

Pros: No permanent changes, easy install, built-in Wi-Fi, works with Alexa/Google/HomeKit.
Cons: Batteries don’t last super long, pricey for a retrofit, doesn’t improve the physical lock itself.

4. Best with Fingerprint: Ultraloq U-Bolt Pro

Price: ~$200 | Grade: Not rated (but solid zinc) | Battery: 4 AA, ~8 months

If you want the James Bond experience, the U-Bolt Pro opens six ways: fingerprint, code, smartphone app, physical key, shake-your-phone, and even an Apple Watch app. The fingerprint sensor is fast and stores up to 20 prints. It’s perfect for families — no one needs to remember a code or carry a key.

I installed this on my front door, and my kids (7 and 10) love using their fingers to get in. The lock is built tough: zinc alloy construction, an anti-peep keypad (you can type random digits before/after your code to confuse onlookers), and a backup keyway. The app isn’t as polished as Schlage’s, but the hardware makes up for it.

Pros: Fingerprint access, anti-peep keypad, works offline, versatile unlocking methods.
Cons: App feels dated, Bluetooth-only without a $50 hub, bulkier design.

5. Best for Google Home Users: Yale Assure Lock 2 (Zigbee/Thread)

Price: ~$250 (with plug-in module) | Grade: ANSI 2 | Battery: 4 AA, ~12 months

The Yale Assure Lock 2 is a modular system: you choose a wireless module (Zigbee, Z-Wave, or Matter/Thread) that slides into the top. For Google Home users who want reliable, local control without cloud dependency, the Thread module is fantastic. The lock itself has no keyhole — just a touchscreen keypad — which eliminates lock bumping entirely.

I tested the Zigbee version with a SmartThings hub for three weeks. The touchscreen wakes instantly, and you can set one-time codes from your phone. The silent operation is a nice touch if you’re coming home late and don’t want to wake anyone. If the battery dies, you can press a 9V battery to the bottom terminals to power it up temporarily.

Pros: Modular for future upgrades, reliable local smart home control, sleek look, excellent battery.
Cons: No physical key (some see this as a pro), touchscreen can be finicky in rain, not the cheapest.

Smart Lock Installation Tips

I’ve installed enough of these to know where the pain points are. Here’s what I wish I’d known on my first attempt.

DIY vs Professional Install

Most smart locks replace your existing deadbolt and use the same holes. If your door is standard (1-3/4" to 2-1/4" thick, with 2-1/8" bore hole), you can install one in about 20 minutes with a Phillips screwdriver. The instructions are clear, and many manufacturers have video walkthroughs.

If your door is older or misaligned, you may need a chisel to widen the strike plate area. That’s when you might call a locksmith — but 90% of people can handle it themselves. Pro tip: before you remove your old lock, open the door and take a photo of the latch and strike plate positions. It’ll save you a headache when aligning the new one.

A Simple Alignment Trick

If your new smart lock motor struggles to turn the deadbolt, the door alignment is off. Instead of moving the whole lock, try adjusting the strike plate on the door frame. Loosen the screws, shift it slightly, and tighten while testing the lock. Sometimes a tiny 1mm adjustment makes the difference between a grinding motor and a smooth lock.

Smart Lock Safety Features You Can’t Ignore

A smart lock is only as secure as the habits around it. Here are a few features that matter more than you think.

  • Auto-lock timer: Set it to lock 30 seconds after the door closes. On models like the Wyze Lock Bolt, this is a lifesaver if you have kids who forget.
  • Entry logs: Check the app periodically to see who opened the door and when. On my August lock, I noticed the dog walker was arriving 15 minutes late — not a security breach, but helpful info.
  • Tamper alerts: Some locks will blare a siren or send a push notification if someone tries to force the keypad or remove the cover. The Schlage Encode Plus does this well.
  • Remote access: Being able to lock/unlock from anywhere isn’t just convenient; it means you can let a trusted neighbor in during an emergency without hiding a key under the mat.

Avoid “Geofencing Only” Unlocks

Some locks offer to unlock automatically when your phone approaches. It’s convenient, but if someone steals your phone, they’re at your door. I recommend using geofencing only with two-factor authentication or combining it with a PIN/code requirement on the phone itself.

Final Thoughts

A good smart lock won’t turn your home into Fort Knox, but it will remove the most common security flaw: human forgetfulness. After months of testing, the Schlage Encode Plus is my top pick for its build quality and Home Key integration, but the Wyze Lock Bolt offers incredible value for less than $100. The best lock for you is the one you’ll actually use — and one that fits your door, your smart home ecosystem, and your budget.

Whichever you choose, take 20 minutes to install it properly, enable auto-lock, and educate everyone in the house on how to use it. When you can close your eyes at night and know your door is locked without getting out of bed, you’ll wonder why you didn’t upgrade sooner.
